teaser: A whole city on a strip of silk you could roll up and carry under your arm.

lesson.text: You were never meant to see this painting all at once. Its first owners laid it on a table, held the roll in the left hand and opened it with the right, about an arm's length at a time. Then they rolled up what they had seen and opened the next stretch. It is a film you wind by hand.

This format is called a handscroll. Here it is a ribbon of silk about 25 centimeters high (10 inches) and more than 5 meters long (17 feet), painted in ink and light color. It shows a day in Bianjing, today's Kaifeng, capital of China's Song dynasty and around the year 1100 one of the largest cities on earth.

People have counted the inhabitants of the scroll. The usual tally is more than 800 human figures, along with dozens of boats, carts, sedan chairs, donkeys, oxen and camels. Many of the people are smaller than a fingernail.

Chinese handscrolls are read from right to left, like Chinese writing of the time. So the story starts at the right-hand end, and it starts quietly. The painter makes you walk into town the way a traveler would, with the noise growing as you go.

lesson.title: Walking into the city
lesson.text: Four stops, from the right end of the scroll to the left, in the order a reader would unroll them.

spots.title: Open country
spots.text: The scroll opens among misty trees and fields outside the city. There is a lot of bare silk here and very little happening: a slow first breath before the crowd.

spots.title: The river
spots.text: The trees give way to the Bian River, the city's supply line. The long dark shapes are heavy cargo boats, the kind that carried grain to the capital, moored along the bank.

spots.title: The bridge
spots.text: A single wooden arch leaps over the water with no pillars beneath it. People called such a bridge a rainbow bridge. This is the busiest spot in the scroll and its dramatic peak.

spots.title: The city streets
spots.text: Past the bridge the buildings crowd together: the city gate, inns, shops and stalls packed along the main street. The empty silk of the opening has completely filled up.

lesson.text: At the bridge, Zhang Zeduan stages a small emergency. A big boat is drifting toward the arch with its mast still being lowered. The crew scrambles with poles, and people on the bridge lean over the rail to shout and throw ropes. After two meters of calm, the scroll suddenly has a plot.

The buildings and boats are drawn in a style called ruled-line painting: the artist used a ruler and fine brush to make beams, planks and rigging as exact as an engineer's plan. Historians of technology study this scroll to learn how Song ships were steered and how such a bridge was fitted together.
A handscroll has no single viewpoint. The painter floats above the scene and moves along with you, so the picture unfolds in time, like a walk, not like a view through a window.

About the artist we know almost nothing. Zhang Zeduan's name comes from a note written on the scroll in 1186, decades later. By then the city he had painted was gone: Bianjing fell to invaders from the north in 1127. For later readers the scroll became a memory of a lost golden age.

Nobody is sure what the title means. Qingming is a spring festival when families sweep their ancestors' graves. But the two characters also mean “bright and peaceful,” so the title may simply praise a calm, well-governed age.
A scroll this famous passed through many hands over nine centuries: emperors, officials, private collectors. In China, owners did not hide that. They signed their admiration directly onto the object.

lesson.title: Nine centuries of owners
lesson.text: Go to the two ends of the scroll, where the pale mounting begins.

spots.title: Seals at the start
spots.text: The small red marks are seals, stamps carved with a name and pressed in red paste. Each one says, in effect, “this was mine” or “I saw this.”

spots.title: Seals at the end
spots.text: More red stamps close the scroll. Beyond this point, later admirers added written comments on extra lengths of paper, so the object kept growing after the painter was done.

lesson.text: The last emperor, Puyi, took the scroll with him when he left the Forbidden City in the 1920s. It vanished in the chaos of war, then turned up in 1950 in a museum storeroom in northeast China, where a curator recognized it among other works. It went home to Beijing, to the Palace Museum.

At the 2010 World Expo in Shanghai, the scroll was shown as a giant animated projection, about thirty times its real size. The tiny figures walked and the boats moved, and day turned into a night lit by lanterns.

The real silk is so fragile that the museum shows it only once every several years, and visitors have queued for hours to file past it. They see it fully unrolled in a long glass case. Its first readers saw less at a time, and probably more: one arm's length, held in the hands, then rolled away.

quiz.question: In which direction is a Chinese handscroll read?
quiz.explanation: The story begins at the right end and is unrolled toward the left.

quiz.question: What marks the dramatic high point of the scroll?
options: The arched bridge, where a boat is in trouble
A fire in the city gate
quiz.explanation: At the rainbow bridge a boat drifts toward the arch while the crew struggles to lower its mast.

quiz.question: What is “ruled-line painting”?
options: Painting only in black and white
Drawing buildings and boats precisely with a ruler and fine brush
quiz.explanation: The ruler let the artist draw beams, planks and rigging with an engineer's precision.

quiz.question: What are the small red marks at the ends of the scroll?
options: Seals stamped by owners and viewers
quiz.explanation: Collectors pressed their seals onto the scroll to record that they had owned or seen it.

quiz.question: How did the first owners look at the scroll?
options: Hung on a wall like a framed picture
On a table, an arm's length at a time
quiz.explanation: A handscroll is unrolled by hand in short sections and rolled up again as you go.

facts.text: The city shown in the scroll was conquered within a few decades of being painted.
facts.explanation: Bianjing fell to northern invaders in 1127, which turned the scroll into a memory of a lost age.

facts.text: The scroll is as tall as a doorway.
facts.explanation: It is only about 25 centimeters high, though more than 5 meters long.

facts.text: Zhang Zeduan's life is thoroughly documented in records from his own time.
facts.explanation: Almost everything known about him comes from a note written on the scroll in 1186.
